column4: Yes, there is one notebook that is easily run from run.sh. It seems like not all of the numbers from the report are easily reproduced in the code though, like some of the data counts.
column5: Move helper files into a separate python file and clean up some unused imports and commented out code.
column6: Overall easy to read. A few sentences have missing words or punctuation. The biggest thing is probably that the figures dont have captions.
column7: Yes, the report has a continuous narrative.
column8: The cleaning is described cleanly, and there is a reason for each choice.
column9: The two questions are decent choices, and there is a reason given for why they were chosen. The maps and the table are understandable. I would have looked at a third question as well.
column10: I think the map nicely shows the distribution of question choices across the US, in a way that shows the nuances across state borders.
column11: Certain areas of the map are difficult to see when there are a lot of overlapping points. This might lead to some information being visually lost.
column12: I agree with using PCA on the data without scaling. The author also gives good reasoning for it. It could have been good if something other than just PCA was also tried.
column13: I like that the plot was colored from east to west, I think that is in interesting approach to tying the plot to the geography.
column14: Perhaps showing multiple views of the PCs would be good.
column15: K-means and hierarchical clustering seems reasonable and it seems to match well with the geography. I also think that the choice of clusters is argued well on the basis of domain knowledge, even though the silhouette score is higher for 5 clusters.
column16: I like the synergy between the bar chart and the map, because it simultaneously shows us where the clusters are located geographically, as well as what the clusters answer across the y'all and soda questions.
column17: Similarly to the earlier geographical map, this one also has a bit of overlap across the groups, which loses some of the visual information in the actual distribution of the clusters across the country, since some points are hidden behind others. Also there is no figure for hierarchical clustering.
column18: They test different starting points, and different subsamples, and the results look stable. Maybe they could have tried to analyze a different amount of clusters as well, to see if 3 is the most stable.

column5: Since an unanswered question becomes all zeros after one-hot encoding, missingness can affect Euclidean distances used by PCA and clustering.
column7: The report has a strong continuous narrative.
column8: The cleaning decisions are clearly described, including invalid state codes, missing coordinates, observations outside the continental U.S., nonresponses, and respondents who answered none of the lexical questions. I also liked that geographic exclusions are applied only when geography is needed.
column9: it would also be interesting to check whether the pattern extends to a third question.
column10: The side-by-side maps are very effective because the regional patterns in Q50 and Q105 can be compared directly.
column11: some local patterns are difficult to see.
column12: I thought the dimensionality-reduction analysis was particularly strong. The author clearly explains why PCA should not be applied directly to the original categorical codes and even demonstrates the problem empirically using Q59.
column13: I liked that the PCA figure does not overstate the separation in the first two components.
column14: Because the PC1-PC2 plot contains tens of thousands of overlapping points, the geographic gradient is somewhat difficult to see.
column15: I think the evidence for exactly three clusters wass not especially strong
column16: I liked the combination of the geographic K-means map and the linguistic response profiles.
column17: I would have liked to see a figure for the hierarchical clustering result as well, such as a dendrogram or a map of its three clusters.
column18: As an additional check, I would vary the number of retained PCs or repeat the analysis under different missing-data restrictions, since these analytical choices may affect the clustering more than random initialization does.
